reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Defined by obesity with chronic daytime hypercapnia and hypoxaemia that is not explained by another cause of hypoventilation
Most patients also have obstructive sleep apnoea, with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, and daytime sleepiness
It should be suspected in an obese patient with an unexplained raised serum bicarbonate reflecting chronic carbon dioxide retention
Untreated disease progresses to pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure (cor pulmonale), and peripheral oedema
Patients are vulnerable to acute-on-chronic respiratory failure, which can be precipitated by infection, sedatives, or high-flow uncontrolled oxygen
Positive airway pressure therapy is the cornerstone of management, alongside sustained weight reduction
It is increasingly relevant as obesity prevalence rises, including in urban India
reference.pathophysiology: Severe obesity increases the mechanical load on the respiratory system through chest wall and abdominal fat, reducing lung volumes and respiratory compliance and increasing the work of breathing. Combined with blunted central ventilatory responsiveness to carbon dioxide and, in most patients, coexisting upper airway obstruction during sleep, this leads to chronic alveolar hypoventilation. Sustained carbon dioxide retention drives renal bicarbonate retention, which further blunts the ventilatory drive. Chronic hypoxaemia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and, over time, pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other intrinsic lung disease
Obstructive sleep apnoea without daytime hypercapnia
Neuromuscular disease causing respiratory muscle weakness
Chest wall disorders such as severe kyphoscoliosis
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas demonstrating daytime hypercapnia and hypoxaemia
Serum bicarbonate as a screening clue to chronic carbon dioxide retention
Sleep study to assess for obstructive sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation
Pulmonary function tests to exclude intrinsic lung disease
Assessment for pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain (ECG and echocardiography)
redFlags: Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure with reduced consciousness
Signs of cor pulmonale and right heart failure
Deterioration after uncontrolled high-flow oxygen or sedative drugs
Severe hypoxaemia or respiratory acidosis requiring urgent ventilatory support
reference.prognosis: Positive airway pressure therapy and weight reduction improve gas exchange, symptoms, and survival; untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from respiratory failure and cor pulmonale.
pitfalls: Attributing hypercapnia to obstructive sleep apnoea alone and missing the hypoventilation syndrome
Giving uncontrolled high-flow oxygen and worsening carbon dioxide retention
Using sedatives that further depress ventilation
Overlooking a raised bicarbonate as an early clue to chronic hypercapnia
management: Positive airway pressure therapy as the cornerstone: CPAP for coexisting obstructive sleep apnoea, or bilevel ventilation for persistent hypercapnia
Sustained weight reduction through lifestyle change, pharmacotherapy or bariatric surgery to reduce respiratory load
Cautious controlled oxygen therapy, avoiding uncontrolled high-flow oxygen that may worsen carbon dioxide retention
Treatment of pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale, including diuretics for right heart failure and peripheral oedema
Avoidance of sedatives and management of precipitants such as infection during acute-on-chronic respiratory failure
Non-invasive ventilation, escalating to invasive ventilatory support, for acute decompensated hypercapnic respiratory failure
Multidisciplinary follow-up with monitoring of daytime gas exchange and adherence to positive airway pressure
